label: Functional Operations
notes: Open by positioning the section as a calculus rather than a catalog. The class already knows the Jensen inequality and epigraph criterion; now each operation must say which certificate survives, what happens to the epigraph, and what domain bookkeeping must be recorded before claiming properness.

label: Operation Ledger
notes: Read this ledger slowly. It separates the proof of convexity from the bookkeeping that students often bundle into the same sentence. A function can be convex but useless for a later theorem if its effective domain vanished, if the value became negative infinity, or if an endpoint extension was silently assumed.

label: Weighted Sums
notes: Use weighted sums as the clean algebraic prototype. The proof is exactly the same inequality repeated with nonnegative multipliers, which explains why a negative coefficient is dangerous. Then shift attention to domains: adding an indicator is not a penalty slogan, it is an extended-real domain restriction.

label: Affine Precomposition
notes: This is the inverse-image operation for functions. Do not ask whether the affine map is one-to-one; it does not matter for convexity because it commutes with averages. What can change is the shape of level sets and the domain, so the rank and pullback domain remain part of the ledger.

label: Pointwise Supremum
notes: Pointwise supremum is best taught visually as an upper envelope, but prove it by epigraphs. The active function can change from one point to another, and that switching is exactly where a graph-only argument feels shaky. Epigraph intersection removes the ambiguity and handles arbitrary families.

label: Max Of Functions
notes: Use finite maxima as the practical version of supremum. Students see the active affine piece change, but the graph never bends downward. Stress the asymmetry: maxima preserve convexity, minima usually do not. That single contrast prevents many false closure claims later.

label: Partial Minimization
notes: Partial minimization is the operation behind eliminating variables from a convex problem. The proof is geometric: project the epigraph of a jointly convex function. Make the warning explicit, because students often confuse convexity of the value function with attainment or boundedness of the inner problem.

label: Infimal Convolution
notes: Define infimal convolution as a best decomposition of x. The point of the diagram is that the variable y is not extra decoration; it is the certificate that says how the total input is split between two convex costs. Convexity is inherited from adding epigraphs.

label: Perspective Transform
notes: Connect the modern word perspective to the section's right scalar multiplication of epigraphs. For positive lambda, the formula is clear. At lambda zero, the formula is not a formula anymore; it is a cone boundary decision, which is why epigraph bookkeeping is safer than informal substitution.

label: Closure Under Limits
notes: Treat limits as a careful consequence, not a magic closure rule. For each fixed pair of points and weight, the Jensen inequality can pass to a pointwise limit when the values are well defined. Then remind the class that lower semicontinuity and closed epigraphs are additional topological properties.

label: Epigraph Arithmetic
notes: This slide is the bookkeeping center of the lecture. The same picture explains several operations once students decide what is being added, intersected, projected, or convexified. Emphasize that the function is read from the lower boundary only after the correct epigraph set operation is complete.

label: Domain Bookkeeping
notes: Make domain bookkeeping feel like part of the theorem, even when it is technically a separate statement. Extended-real convex analysis is powerful because constraints are functions, but that power comes with arithmetic rules. A clean proof of convexity can still leave an empty domain or an unbounded infimum.

label: Counterexamples
notes: Use this slide to sharpen the hypotheses. Each failure is a near miss: negative scaling looks like scaling, minimum looks like maximum, decreasing composition looks like composition, and partial minimization looks harmless until the value runs away. Ask students to name the missing assumption before reading the explanation.

label: Computational Rule Checker
notes: Turn the lecture into a small diagnostic program. The checker first verifies the theorem hypotheses, then records the epigraph move and domain rule, and only then samples a midpoint residual. The finite checks are not proofs; they are sanity tests that keep examples honest and catch swapped signs.

label: Recap
notes: Close with a repeatable inspection prompt. Students should not memorize the operations as separate facts; they should ask how averages survive, which epigraph set operation is responsible, and what domain or properness warning remains. That habit prepares them for conjugates, gauges, support functions, and duality.
